text: The previous lesson ran a circuit and got back shot counts — an estimate built from repeated sampling. But simulation can also hand you something no real quantum computer ever can: the exact, complete quantum state itself, with no sampling involved at all.

Statevector computes the full complex amplitude vector of a circuit directly, with no sampling and no measurement gates in the circuit at all. For a Bell-state circuit, the exact result is amplitude 0.7071068 on 00 and on 11, and exactly zero on 01 and 10. This is the one thing a real quantum computer can never hand you directly — you cannot read out an amplitude by looking at it, only by measuring and collapsing it to a classical bit.

The alternative is to add measurement gates and run the circuit many times — loosely called QASM-style simulation, after the older backend name. This is the execution model real hardware is stuck with: run, measure, repeat, build up statistics. A real seeded run at 4096 shots gives something like 00: 2021, 11: 2075, with 01 and 10 still at exactly zero.

Put the two results side by side. The statevector approach says, with certainty, P(00) and P(11) are exactly 0.5. The shot-based approach observed roughly 0.4934 and 0.5066 — close, but not exact, and it would be a different 'not exact' on a different run. Statevector simulation tells you the exact ground truth; shot-based simulation, and real hardware, only ever give you a noisy estimate of it. That's true even here, where the simulator itself is completely noiseless — the only source of that gap is statistical sampling noise from a finite number of shots.
Next lesson puts a real formula behind 'more shots, less noise' — how standard error shrinks as shots increase, and at what rate, so you can decide how many shots a real experiment actually needs.
